findings.reason: without the followup naming them, §27 and §28 are reachable only by a reader who cross-checks every section declaration against the followup, which is the gap three earlier followups in this plan were each found to have left.
findings.text: f-wftl-006, the plan's only open followup, is titled "Build §9, §22, §24 and §26" while s27 and s28 are newly declared implementable at plan.html:23 and are named by no followup, and the followup's data-recommends-skill is empty, so a coordinator driving the plan from its open followup dispatches neither new section

findings.reason: the failure the section exists to end is a landing lane held by one slow job, and a bound that is never enforced is that same lane held until the scheduler kills it, so a gate that never plants an over-bound or cancelled job cannot show the bound is honoured.
findings.text: s27's deliverable requires that "a job that fails, exceeds its bound or is cancelled refuses only its own run, naming the job id and its log", but the done-when exercises one of those three dispositions, "a job reported failed", so an implementation that never settles a cancelled or over-bound job — leaving its run pending indefinitely — passes the whole gate

findings.reason: s28 removes the lease-holding that currently stops two sweeps duplicating the same minutes, so the suppression becomes the only thing that re-judges a run once its review changes; a head-only key leaves a re-reviewed run refused for good, a stall worse than the one the section removes.
findings.text: s28's deliverable suppresses a re-attempt only "while the run's head, its stored review and the refusal's own inputs are unchanged", but the done-when varies the head alone ("is judged again once its head moves") and never changes the stored review or the refusal's inputs, so an implementation whose suppression key covers only the head passes every case

response_events.note: f-wftl-006 is resolved and replaced by a followup naming §27 and §28 with an invocation that builds §27.

rubric_items.anchors_resolve: pass — every write path resolves (`reckon/crew/queue_landing.py`, `reckon/crew/landing_measure.py`, `reckon/crew/admission/landing.py`, `reckon/crew/admission/service.py`, `reckon/crew/resumption.py`, `reckon/crew/recovery_review_acceptance.py`), both named test modules are absent as new files, and s28's cited stack resolves at `recovery_review_acceptance.py:358`, `recovery_review_acceptance.py:250` and `merge.py:845`.
rubric_items.done_when: a finding — s27's deliverable names three dispositions for a job that yields no measured pair (fails, exceeds its bound, is cancelled) and its gate exercises one of them; s28's suppression rule is keyed on three inputs and its gate varies one.
rubric_items.evidence_paths: pass — both sections write into the plan's durable evidence record, their base arms run on `all_debug`, and s27's live pass is recorded in the worker's manifest under the run directory rather than a node-local temporary path.
rubric_items.naming: pass — both test module names and every symbol the sections name state the mechanism, carrying no plan label, stage name, ticket number or version tag.
rubric_items.reasoning: pass — each stated root cause matches its cited evidence, checked against the repository: the blocking submit is the `--wait` argument at `reckon/crew/landing_measure.py:620`, and the lease is taken around the whole promotion job including the acceptance commit check at `reckon/crew/resumption.py:2178-2181`, so the py-spy stack s28 quotes is the code as it stands; both endpoints are obtainable from a stub scheduler and a temporary crew home, and neither section prescribes a code path, step sequence or formula beyond the behaviour its gate measures.
rubric_items.single_goal: pass — s27 is one goal (a landing that needs a measurement never blocks the lander), its width bound, restart adoption and failure isolation being facets of that goal, and s28 is one goal (a sweep holds a run's promotion lease only while it promotes); each is closed on one gate.
